An allocator for cannot be moved, without updating the pointers to the
allocated memory.

In contrast to , allows zero-sized allocations. If an underlying
allocator does not support this (like jemalloc) or responds by returning a null pointer
(such as ), this must be caught by the implementation.

Attempts to allocate a block of memory.
On success, returns a meeting the size and alignment guarantees of .

The returned block may have a larger size than specified by , and may or may
not have its contents initialized.
The returned block of memory remains valid as long as it is and the shorter of:
the borrow-checker lifetime of the allocator type itself.
as long as the allocator and all its clones have not been dropped.

Returning indicates that either memory is exhausted or does not meet
allocator’s size or alignment constraints.

Implementations are encouraged to return on memory exhaustion rather than panicking or
aborting, but this is not a strict requirement. (Specifically: it is to implement
this trait atop an underlying native allocation library that aborts on memory exhaustion.)

Clients wishing to abort computation in response to an allocation error are encouraged to
call the function, rather than directly invoking or similar.

Returns a new containing a pointer and the actual size of the allocated
memory. The pointer is suitable for holding data described by . To accomplish
this, the allocator may extend the allocation referenced by to fit the new layout.

If this returns , then ownership of the memory block referenced by has been
transferred to this allocator. Any access to the old is Undefined Behavior, even if the
allocation was grown in-place. The newly returned pointer is the only valid pointer
for accessing this memory now.
